title: Occasion and publication
short: Composed in July 1816 in the valley of Chamonix and printed at the end of History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817), dated (wrongly) 'June 23, 1816'.
body: Shelley, Mary Godwin and Claire Clairmont toured Chamonix from about 21 to 27 July 1816, during the summer spent near Byron on Lake Geneva. The poem was first printed as the conclusion of the Shelleys' History of a Six Weeks' Tour (1817), subtitled 'Lines written in the Vale of Chamouni'; the printed date of June 23 conflicts with the travel record, and editors place composition in late July. The preface says the poem was composed under the immediate impression of the scene and claims to imitate its 'untameable wildness and inaccessible solemnity'. A rough earlier version survives in the Scrope Davies Notebook, discovered in a London bank vault in 1976.

sources.cite: [Mary and Percy Shelley], History of a Six Weeks' Tour (London: Hookham and Ollier, 1817), Preface and 'Mont Blanc. Lines written in the Vale of Chamouni'; Letter IV (Shelley to Peacock, July 1816)

title: The everlasting universe of things / Flows through the mind
short: The opening puts the relation of mind and world in the form of a river: the universe flows through the mind, which adds its own feeble 'tribute'.
body: The first section is a single extended figure. The 'universe of things' streams through the mind like a great river, and the mind's own contribution, 'from secret springs', is like a brook that joins it 'with a sound but half its own'. The image belongs to a philosophical debate Shelley knew from Locke, Hume, Berkeley and Sir William Drummond: whether we know a world outside the mind, or only the impressions that flow through it. Wasserman read the poem as Shelley's working-out of a sceptical idealism, while other critics stress its uncertainty. The landscape that follows, the Arve rushing through its ravine, literally enacts the opening figure.

title: Ravine of Arve
short: The Arve is the glacial river that drains the Mont Blanc massif and flows through the valley of Chamonix towards Geneva.
body: Shelley's letter to Peacock describes the road along the Arve, swollen with rain and roaring through a gorge. The poem's second section addresses the ravine as 'thou', making it the outward counterpart of the mind in section I: just as thought receives the stream of things, the ravine is the 'path' of the river's ceaseless sound and motion. The Arve's 'commotion' and its 'giant brood of pines' make the valley a scene of the natural sublime, in the sense of Burke's Enquiry (1757): vastness, obscurity, power and danger producing awe.

anchor: Where Power in likeness of the Arve comes down
title: Power
short: The capitalised 'Power' is the poem's name for the unknown force behind phenomena; it descends in the likeness of the river from a 'secret throne'.
body: Shelley avoids the word 'God'. Power comes down 'in likeness of' the Arve, as the Holy Spirit descends in the likeness of a dove (Luke 3:22), from 'ice-gulfs' that hide its 'secret throne'. The poem never sees Power directly, only its manifestations, and section IV states that 'Power dwells apart in its tranquillity, / Remote, serene, and inaccessible'. Critics disagree whether Power is a sceptic's name for unknown natural necessity, a neutral force indifferent to humanity, or something like Shelley's 'Intellectual Beauty' (the hymn of the same summer). Its final form is 'The secret strength of things / Which governs thought'.

title: unsculptured image
short: The veil of spray over the waterfall robes a shape no artist has carved; nature's forms are like statues, but unmade by human hands.
body: The 'ethereal waterfall' (in the letters, the falls of the valley such as those Shelley saw near Servoz) is veiled in spray with rainbows, and the veil suggests a robed statue beneath. 'Unsculptured' implies both natural and inexpressible: the image beneath has never been shaped, so the veil may cover nothing, or something beyond representation. The figure of the veil recurs in Shelley, most famously in the sonnet 'Lift not the painted veil which those who live / Call Life', and in this poem in 'The veil of life and death' (l. 54).

title: my own separate fantasy
short: Gazing at the ravine, the poet reflects on his own mind, which 'passively' receives and actively 'renders' influences in an 'unremitting interchange'.
body: The lines turn the poem from description to self-reflection, and they echo Wordsworth's language in 'Tintern Abbey' of what the eye and ear 'half create, / And what perceive'. 'Fantasy' here means the imagination or the image-making faculty. 'Renders and receives' describes the mind as both giving back and taking in. The passage is notoriously hard to construe: its wandering thoughts float over the ravine and rest in 'the still cave of the witch Poesy', and the syntax of ll. 41-48 is disputed. Shelley's reworking of Wordsworth's ideas of mind and nature is central to readings of the poem.

title: the still cave of the witch Poesy
short: Poetry is a witch in a cave, where thoughts seek 'shadows' and 'ghosts' of things, a Platonic image of art as knowledge by images.
body: The cave recalls Plato's allegory of the cave (Republic VII), in which prisoners see only shadows of real things; it also suggests the oracular caves of classical prophecy. Poesy, the poetic faculty, is a 'witch' because it conjures images. The poet's thoughts seek among the shadows 'some shade of thee, / Some phantom, some faint image' of the ravine, until the mind recalls them and the ravine is suddenly present: 'thou art there!' The passage is Shelley's account of how poetic images both represent and fall short of their objects, a theme he developed in A Defence of Poetry (1821).

anchor: Some say that gleams of a remoter world
title: Some say that gleams of a remoter world / Visit the soul in sleep
short: Section III begins with doubt: perhaps death is sleep, and the world of dreams 'mightier' than waking; the poet does not know whether he wakes or dreams.
body: The 'some say' introduces a received belief, possibly the Platonic or Wordsworthian idea (the 'Immortality Ode') that intimations of another world reach the soul in sleep or childhood. The poet then asks whether some 'unknown omnipotence' has drawn back 'The veil of life and death', or whether he lies in dream. The spirit 'fails', driven like a cloud among 'viewless gales' (invisible winds; 'viewless' is a poetic word found in Shakespeare and Milton). The uncertainty is characteristic: Shelley's poem moves by questions, not assertions, which is why critics have read it both as sceptical and as quasi-religious.

anchor: The veil of life and death
title: The veil of life and death
short: The boundary between life and death, appearance and reality, is figured as a veil that some power might lift.
body: Veils in Shelley usually mark the limit of human knowledge; to lift one is either to see truth or to discover emptiness. The image links section III to the veiled waterfall of section II and anticipates the mountain's appearance, 'Far, far above', which is the poem's nearest approach to an unveiled vision. Mont Blanc itself, 'still, snowy, and serene', is seen but does not explain itself.

anchor: And the wolf tracts her there
title: And the wolf tracts her there
short: 'Tracts' (the 1817 reading) is usually taken as 'tracks', i.e. follows the eagle, or follows the trail; some editors print 'tracks'.
body: The 1817 printing in History of a Six Weeks' Tour reads 'tracts', which the archive keeps. Editors have either emended it to 'tracks' or explained 'tracts' as an older form of 'tracks' or 'traces', meaning that the wolf follows the eagle to scavenge the hunter's bone. The detail makes the 'desert peopled by the storms alone' a place where only predators and the dead remain, preparing for the hideously heaped shapes of the next lines. Students should note which text their edition follows.

title: the old Earthquake-daemon
short: Shelley asks whether the shattered landscape was the toy of an earthquake spirit or the work of a 'sea / Of fire': geological theories of the earth's violent past.
body: 'Daemon' in its Greek sense is a spirit, neither good nor evil. The questions glance at contemporary geological debates: whether mountains were raised by subterranean fire and upheaval (the Plutonist view associated with James Hutton) or deposited by water. Shelley's letter from Chamonix discusses Buffon's 'sublime but gloomy theory' that the earth will at last be frozen, which also informs section IV's advancing glaciers. 'None can reply, all seems eternal now' expresses the limits of such speculation: the mountain gives no answer.

anchor: Which teaches awful doubt, or faith so mild
title: awful doubt, or faith so mild ... But for such faith
short: The wilderness teaches doubt, or a faith so mild that, 'But for such faith' (except through it), man might be reconciled with nature; the syntax is disputed.
body: The 'mysterious tongue' of the wilderness speaks to some of 'awful doubt' (awe-inspiring scepticism) and to others of a mild faith. Line 79 is a crux. 'But for' can mean 'only by means of', so that such faith reconciles man with nature, or 'were it not for', so that faith is the obstacle and doubt the path to reconciliation. The second reading fits Shelley's hostility to conventional religion: a sceptical awe would reconcile humanity with nature, but a mild faith prevents it. Editors and critics have argued for both readings, and the line is best read as deliberately poised.

anchor: Large codes of fraud and woe
title: to repeal / Large codes of fraud and woe
short: The mountain's voice can 'repeal' the codes of fraud and woe, the religious and political systems that oppress humanity; only the wise interpret it.
body: 'Repeal' is a parliamentary word: the mountain's silent lesson abolishes oppressive laws and creeds, which for Shelley included both despotic government and the religion of a vengeful creator. That week at Chamonix Shelley entered his name in hotel registers with the Greek word atheos ('atheist'), an act reported by later visitors such as Southey, so the political and religious reading of the lines is well grounded. The voice is 'not understood / By all': only 'the wise, and great, and good' can 'Interpret, or make felt, or deeply feel' it, three different relations to truth (the philosopher's, the poet's, the feeling heart's).

title: the daedal earth
short: 'Daedal' means variously and skilfully made; the phrase comes from Lucretius's 'daedala tellus', the inventive earth that brings forth flowers.
body: The adjective derives from Daedalus, the legendary craftsman, via Latin daedalus, 'cunningly wrought'. Lucretius opens De rerum natura with an invocation to Venus, for whom 'daedala tellus' sends up sweet flowers. Shelley admired Lucretius, the poet of materialist philosophy, and uses 'daedal' in several poems, including Prometheus Unbound. The allusion is apt here: section IV lists the living world of fields, lakes and creatures, which 'Are born and die' in endless revolution, a Lucretian picture of a nature without providence.

anchor: Power dwells apart in its tranquillity
title: Power dwells apart in its tranquillity
short: Against the turmoil of birth and death, Power is remote and serene, like the gods of Epicurus who dwell apart, untouched by the world.
body: The line sets an immovable source against everything that moves: all things 'revolve, subside, and swell', but Power is 'Remote, serene, and inaccessible'. Many commentators compare the Epicurean gods described by Lucretius, who live in tranquil detachment from human affairs. The mountain itself, 'the naked countenance of earth', is said to 'Teach the adverting mind' (the mind that turns towards it, attends). What it teaches is ambiguous: indifference, or a power so far beyond human values that it neither punishes nor rewards.

title: The glaciers creep / Like snakes that watch their prey
short: The glaciers creep like snakes and build a 'city of death' that destroys forest, creature and dwelling, as Shelley's letter from Chamonix describes.
body: In his letter to Peacock Shelley described the glaciers advancing on the valley, overthrowing forests and fields, and he mentioned Buffon's theory of a future frozen globe. The poem turns those observations into a vision of nature's destructive power. The glaciers are a 'flood of ruin' that 'Rolls its perpetual stream', destroying the 'dwelling-place / Of insects, beasts, and birds' and making 'The race / Of man' flee. The phrase 'their place is not known' echoes Psalm 103:16 ('the place thereof shall know it no more'). Yet the same ice feeds 'one majestic River, / The breath and blood of distant lands', so destruction and life come from one source.

title: The secret strength of things / Which governs thought
short: The poem's final name for Power: an unseen strength that governs thought and is a law to the heavens, and that inhabits the mountain.
body: Section V returns to the summit, where snows fall unseen and winds and lightning act 'innocently' in silence. Shelley stresses that none beholds them: the mountain's power works without witnesses. The 'secret strength of things' resembles the Lucretian or Newtonian idea of natural law, but Shelley also says it 'governs thought', closing the circle with the poem's opening, in which the universe flows through the mind. 'Infinite dome / Of heaven' recalls the 'dome' imagery of his other poems, such as the 'dome of many-coloured glass' in Adonais.

title: If to the human mind's imaginings / Silence and solitude were vacancy?
short: The final question: what would mountain, earth and stars be if the human imagination found only emptiness in silence and solitude?
body: The ending is one of the most discussed in Romantic poetry. One reading is humanist: the mountain matters only because the imagination fills its silence with meaning, so mind confers value on nature. Another is sceptical: the question admits that silence and solitude may be vacancy, and that the imagination may be projecting. A third, Wasserman's, takes the line as an affirmation that the mind's imaginings reveal the power genuinely present in things. The rhetorical question, without a question of fact, leaves the poem poised between these, and its last word, 'vacancy', is a hard word to end on.

anchor: Thine earthly rainbows stretched across the sweep
title: Form: irregular rhyme
short: Five numbered sections of blank-verse-like pentameter with irregular, unpredictable rhyme, imitating the 'untameable wildness' the preface claims.
body: The poem looks like blank verse, but rhymes occur at irregular intervals and sometimes at a distance (as 'sweep' and 'sleep', ll. 25-27, or 'tame' and 'came' within section II), so the ear hears an order that it cannot predict. Critics connect this with the preface's claim to imitate the scene's 'wildness'; it also suggests the Pindaric ode, and some readers hear an answer to Coleridge's 'Hymn Before Sun-rise, in the Vale of Chamouni' (1802), whose pious apostrophe to the mountain Shelley's sceptical poem revises. The five sections progress from mind and ravine to the summit's secret power.
